title: IdentiFlight automated curtailment at Top of the World wind facility, Wyoming: 82% eagle fatality reduction claimed, cut to 50% with a CI spanning an increase by a USGS reanalysis
summary: McClure et al. 2021 reported an 82% (75-89%) lower eagle fatality rate after IdentiFlight camera-triggered curtailment in Wyoming; Huso & Dalthorp 2023 recalculated 50% (-159%, 89%). Contested.
account: McClure et al. (Journal of Applied Ecology, published online 31 January 2021) tested an automated curtailment system, a camera system that detects flying objects, classifies them and decides whether to curtail individual turbines, at the Top of the World Windpower Facility in Wyoming, USA, in a before-after-control-impact design against a control site 15 km away; after correcting for carcass detection, they estimated fatalities fell 63% at the treatment site while rising 113% at the control site, 'an 82% (75%-89%) reduction in the fatality rate at the treatment site relative to the control site'. The same authors, in Ecological Solutions and Evidence (2022), reanalysed with additional data and reported an 85% reduction (95% highest density interval 12% to 100%) with the IdentiFlight system. Huso and Dalthorp of the US Geological Survey (Journal of Applied Ecology, 30 August 2023) identified four major errors (ignoring annual variation, unfounded causal inference from one treatment year at one site, inflated effect size, inconsistent data with 7 of 42 fatalities excluded) and gave a corrected estimate of 50% (-159%, 89%) reduction or possible increase, concluding that the claim is not supported by the data. The activation date of the system is not given in the fetched abstracts; the date used is the 2021 publication date.
purpose: Detect approaching eagles with cameras and classification software and curtail individual turbines to avoid collisions; the claimed reduction in fatalities is the intended effect.
system: IdentiFlight automated eagle detection and turbine curtailment (camera system that detects, classifies and triggers curtailment)
developer: IdentiFlight (device marketed as Identiflight; company not further named in the fetched abstracts)
deployer: Top of the World Windpower Facility, Wyoming (operator not named in the fetched abstracts)
location: Top of the World Windpower Facility, Wyoming, USA
segment: Wind power operator with conservation research partners
taxonomy_note: Eagle fatality reduction fits environmental sustainability. The benefit is contested: the original and follow-up studies (The Peregrine Fund, WEST and USGS authors, Murdock Charitable Trust funding; no IdentiFlight affiliation listed in Crossref) claim 82-85% reductions, while an independent USGS reanalysis finds the corrected interval spans an increase. The depth ratings reflect the claim as made, with the contestation stated here and in the AI role statement.

ratings.reason: For the facility, the studies report a large fall in eagle fatalities (82% then 85%) that would reduce protected-species take; the reanalysis says the corrected estimate of 50% has an interval spanning an increase, so the organisational benefit is uncertain.
One facility and, per the reanalysis, one treatment year; any population-level benefit to eagles is unproven and the effect size is disputed.

ai_role.statement: The camera-based detection and classification system is the mechanism that triggers curtailment, so any fatality reduction is attributable to it together with the curtailment policy; however, the independent USGS reanalysis (Huso and Dalthorp 2023) attributes the reported 82% effect to four methodological errors and finds little evidence of reduction once corrected, while the original authors' 2022 reanalysis reaffirms an 85% reduction with a wide interval. The benefit is therefore contested between peer-reviewed sources and not verified.
